items.stem: Which of the following mixtures are correctly classified as homogeneous (Hm) and heterogeneous (Ht)? Choose the correct option. (i) Air — Hm, Milk — Ht, Sugar solution — Hm, Smoke — Hm (ii) Brass — Ht, Fog — Ht, Vinegar — Ht, Muddy water — Hm (iii) Copper sulfate solution — Hm, Salt solution — Hm, Milk — Hm, Bronze — Hm (iv) Muddy water — Ht, Milk — Ht, Blood — Ht, Brass — Hm
items.answer: Option (iv) is the correct choice. Muddy water, milk, and blood are all heterogeneous mixtures (specifically suspensions or colloids) because their compositions are not uniform throughout, whereas brass is an alloy, which is considered a homogeneous mixture of metals.

items.stem: Choose the correct options, and explain the reason for the correct and incorrect options. Which among the following mixtures show the Tyndall Effect? A mixture of: (a) air and dust particles (b) copper sulfate and water (c) starch and water (d) acetone and water (i) a and b (ii) b and d (iii) a and c (iv) c and d
items.answer: Option (iii) a and c is correct. The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam of light by particles in a colloid or fine suspension. A mixture of air and dust particles (an aerosol) and a mixture of starch and water are both colloids, possessing particles large enough to scatter light, making them correct options. On the other hand, copper sulfate in water and acetone in water form true solutions; their solute particles are too small (less than 1 nm in diameter) to scatter light, making them incorrect options.

items.stem: A mixture can be categorised as a solution, a suspension, or a colloid, each possessing distinct properties. Utilise the words or phrases provided in the box to fill in the Table. Words and phrases may be used more than once. Words and Phrases: Large-sized particles; Particles remain evenly distributed; Small-sized particles (less than 1 nm diameter); Moderate-sized particles (1–1000 nm); Settles down when left undisturbed (more than 1000 nm in diameter); Does not settle down; Scatters light; Separates by filtration; Transparent; Salt solution; Milk; Sand in water; Smoke; Heterogeneous mixture; Cannot be separated by filtration; Mud; Butter; Brass. Complete the Table by giving the Properties and the Examples for each of Solution, Suspension and Colloid.
items.answer: Solution — Properties: homogeneous mixture; particle size less than 1 nm (small particles); transparent; particles do not scatter light; stable, particles do not settle down; cannot be separated by filtration. Examples: salt solution, sugar solution. Suspension — Properties: heterogeneous mixture; particle size more than 1000 nm (large particles); opaque; particles scatter light strongly; unstable, particles settle down on standing; can be separated by filtration. Examples: muddy water, sand in water. Colloid — Properties: heterogeneous (appears homogeneous); particle size between 1 nm and 1000 nm; translucent; particles scatter light (Tyndall effect); quite stable, particles do not settle down; cannot be separated by ordinary filtration. Examples: milk, butter, smoke.

items.stem: Solve the following problems: (i) A cake recipe uses dry ingredients, namely 75 g of sugar for 420 g of all-purpose flour and 5 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate. Express the concentration of each component in the mixture using an appropriate method. (ii) A brass alloy contains 70% copper by mass. Calculate the quantities of copper and zinc present in 120 g of brass.
items.answer: (i) We can use the mass by mass percentage (% m/m) method. First, calculate the total mass of the mixture: 75 g (sugar) + 420 g (flour) + 5 g (sodium hydrogencarbonate) = 500 g. Concentration of sugar = (Mass of sugar / Total mass) × 100 = (75 / 500) × 100 = 15% m/m. Concentration of all-purpose flour = (Mass of flour / Total mass) × 100 = (420 / 500) × 100 = 84% m/m. Concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate = (Mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate / Total mass) × 100 = (5 / 500) × 100 = 1% m/m. (ii) Mass of the brass alloy is 120 g. Quantity of copper = 70% of total mass = (70 / 100) × 120 g = 84 g. Assuming the rest of the alloy is zinc, the percentage of zinc is 100% - 70% = 30%. Quantity of zinc = 30% of total mass = (30 / 100) × 120 g = 36 g (alternatively, 120 g total - 84 g copper = 36 g zinc).

items.stem: The label on a cooking oil pack says one litre (910 g). If this oil is mixed with water, will it form a separate layer? If so, which substance will be on top? How will you separate the two layers? Also, draw the diagram of the apparatus used.
items.answer: Yes, the oil and water will form separate layers because they are immiscible liquids. Based on the label, the density of the oil is 910 g per 1000 mL (0.91 g/mL), which is less than the density of water (approximately 1 g/mL). Because it is lighter, the cooking oil will float and form the top layer. The two layers can be separated using a separating funnel.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Solutions do not exhibit the Tyndall effect. Reason (R): The particles in solutions are larger than 100 nm, so they cannot scatter light. Choose the correct option: (i) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. (ii) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (iii) A is true, but R is false. (iv) A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Option (iii) is the correct choice. The assertion is true because true solutions are homogeneous mixtures that do not scatter light. However, the reason is false because the solute particles in a solution are extremely small (less than 1 nm in diameter), not larger than 100 nm; it is precisely their small size that prevents them from scattering a light beam.

items.stem: How would you separate the mixtures given in Table? Mention the reason for choosing your method. If a mixture cannot be separated, explain why. The table lists, against the columns Mixture, Method of separation and Reason for selection: mud from muddy water; plasma from other components in the blood sample; naphthalene and sand; chalk powder and common salt; common salt and water; oil from water; pigments of the flower.
items.answer:
Mud from muddy water — Filtration. Mud particles are insoluble solids suspended in the water and are large enough to be retained by a filter paper.
Plasma from other components in the blood sample — Centrifugation. Spinning the blood at high speeds applies centrifugal force, causing the heavier blood cells to settle at the bottom while the lighter liquid plasma remains at the top due to density differences.
Naphthalene and sand — Sublimation. Naphthalene is a sublimable substance that transitions directly from a solid to a vapour on heating, leaving the non-sublimable sand behind.
Chalk powder and common salt — Dissolution in water followed by filtration. Common salt is soluble in water while chalk powder is insoluble. After dissolving the salt, filtration separates the solid chalk, and the pure salt can be recovered later by evaporating the filtrate.
Common salt and water — Evaporation. Heating the solution causes the volatile solvent (water) to vaporize, leaving behind the non-volatile solid solute (common salt).
Oil from water — Separating funnel. Oil and water are immiscible liquids with different densities, meaning they do not mix and naturally separate into distinct layers that can be drained off one by one.
Pigments of the flower — Paper chromatography. The different coloured pigments have varying degrees of solubility in the solvent; as the solvent travels up the chromatography paper, the more soluble pigments move faster and separate from the others.

items.stem: Two miscible liquids, A and B, are present in a mixture. The boiling point of A is 60 °C and the boiling point of B is 90 °C. Suggest a method to separate them. Also, draw a labelled diagram of the method suggested.
items.answer: Since A and B are miscible liquids with a boiling point difference of 30 °C (which is greater than the required 25 °C minimum difference), they can be successfully separated using the process of simple distillation.

items.stem: Compare evaporation, crystallization and distillation. In which situation, would you prefer each of these over the others?
items.answer: Comparison: 1. Evaporation involves heating a solution to vaporize the volatile solvent, leaving behind a non-volatile solid residue. 2. Crystallization involves slowly cooling a hot, saturated solution so that the solid solute separates out as pure, regular geometric crystals. 3. Distillation involves heating a liquid mixture until the component with the lower boiling point vaporizes, then routing that vapour through a condenser to cool it back into a liquid state for collection. Situations for preference: 1. Evaporation is preferred when you only need to recover a simple, heat-stable solid solute from a solution and do not care about capturing the solvent that evaporates away. 2. Crystallization is preferred over evaporation when obtaining a highly pure solid is necessary, especially if the solid might decompose upon dry heating (like sugar) or if soluble impurities need to be left behind in the remaining liquid. 3. Distillation is preferred when you need to separate and recover both the liquid solvent and the solid solute, or when you need to separate two miscible liquids that have a sufficient difference in their boiling points (at least 25 °C).

items.stem: Blood is an example of a colloidal mixture. (i) What would happen if blood behaved like a true suspension inside the body? (ii) In a blood sample, identify the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium.
items.answer: (i) If blood were a true suspension, the heavier blood cells would settle out of the liquid due to gravity whenever blood flow slowed or stopped. This would lead to blockages in blood vessels, prevent oxygen and nutrients from reaching tissues, and ultimately cause the circulatory system to fail. (ii) In a blood sample, the dispersed phase consists of the blood cells (such as red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets), and the dispersion medium is the liquid plasma in which they are suspended.

items.stem: You are given a mixture of sand, common salt and naphthalene. The figure depicts various steps used to separate the components of this mixture. Identify and write down the correct sequence of separation techniques.
items.answer: Based on the visual cues in the figure the correct sequence of separation techniques is: 1. Sublimation (heating the mixture with an inverted funnel to separate the sublimable naphthalene). 2. Filtration (pouring the remaining mixture, after adding water to dissolve the salt, through filter paper to remove the insoluble sand). 3. Evaporation (heating the collected filtrate in a dish to boil off the water and leave behind the common salt).

items.stem: Why is distillation an effective method for separating a mixture of water and acetone?
items.answer: Distillation is effective because water and acetone are miscible liquids with a large difference in their boiling points. Acetone boils at approximately 56 °C, while water boils at 100 °C. Because this difference (44 °C) is greater than 25 °C, the acetone readily vaporizes first upon heating and can be condensed and collected as a pure liquid well before the water begins to vaporize significantly.

items.stem: Answer the following questions with the help of the data given in the Table. Table: solubility of various salts, in g per 100 g of water, at 10 °C, 20 °C, 30 °C, 40 °C, 60 °C and 80 °C respectively — Potassium nitrate: 21, 32, 45, 62, 106, 167; Sodium chloride: 36, 36, 36.3, 36.5, 37, 37; Potassium chloride: 35, 35, 37.4, 40, 46, 54; Ammonium chloride: 24, 37, 41, 41, 55, 66. (i) What mass of potassium nitrate would be needed to prepare its saturated solution in 50 g of water at 40 °C? (ii) A student makes a saturated solution of potassium chloride in water at 80 °C and leaves the solution to cool at room temperature (25 °C). What would she observe as the solution cools? Explain. (iii) What is the effect of a change in temperature on the solubility of salts? Also, compare the changes in the solubility of the four given salts with increasing temperature from 10 °C to 80 °C.
items.answer:
(i) According to the table, the solubility of potassium nitrate at 40 °C is 62 g per 100 g of water. To prepare a saturated solution in half that amount of water (50 g), you would need half the mass of the salt, which is 31 g of potassium nitrate.
(ii) She would observe solid crystals forming in the solution. This happens because the solubility of solid salts generally decreases as temperature drops. The water can hold 54 g of potassium chloride at 80 °C but only around 36 g at 25 °C, forcing the excess dissolved salt to separate out of the solution in crystalline form.
(iii) Generally, an increase in temperature increases the solubility of solid salts in water. Comparing the given salts from 10 °C to 80 °C: Potassium nitrate shows a massive increase in solubility (from 21 g to 167 g). Ammonium chloride and Potassium chloride show steady, moderate increases in solubility. Sodium chloride is unique among the four, as its solubility shows almost no change, remaining relatively constant (increasing slightly from 36 g to 37 g).

items.stem: Three students, A, B and C, are preparing sugar solutions for an experiment. Student A dissolves 20 g of sugar in 80 g of water. Student B dissolves 20 g of sugar in 100 g of water. Student C dissolves 30 g of sugar in 80 g of water. (i) Calculate the mass percentage (% m/m) concentration of sugar in each student’s solution. (ii) Whose solution is the most concentrated? Explain why.
items.answer:
(i) The mass percentage is the mass of the solute divided by the total mass of the solution, multiplied by one hundred. Student A dissolved 20 g of sugar in 80 g of water, so that solution has a total mass of one hundred grams and its concentration is 20 per cent m/m. Student B dissolved 20 g of sugar in 100 g of water, so that solution has a total mass of one hundred and twenty grams and its concentration is 16.67 per cent m/m. Student C dissolved 30 g of sugar in 80 g of water, so that solution has a total mass of one hundred and ten grams and its concentration is 27.27 per cent m/m.
(ii) Student C’s solution is the most concentrated. This is because it has the highest mass percentage (27.27 per cent), meaning it contains the highest proportion of solute relative to the total mass of the solution compared to the mixtures prepared by students A and B.

items.stem: Examine the figure. (i) Identify the separation technique marked as ‘S’. (ii) Label the apparatus A, B and C. (iii) Which of the following mixtures can be separated by the technique identified above? Use the data given in the Table. Mixtures: (a) water—acetone (b) water—salt (c) acetone—alcohol (d) sand—salt (e) alcohol—chloroform (f) alcohol—benzene. Table: Boiling points of some compounds — Water 100 °C, Acetone 56 °C, Alcohol 78 °C, Chloroform 61 °C, Benzene 80 °C.
items.answer: (i) The separation technique marked as ‘S’ is Distillation. (ii) A: Distillation flask; B: Water condenser; C: Water inlet (where cold water enters the condenser jacket). (iii) Mixture (a) water-acetone can be separated by this technique. Distillation is effective for separating miscible liquids that have a boiling point difference of at least 25 °C. Using the provided table, the difference between the boiling points of water (100 °C) and acetone (56 °C) is 44 °C, making it suitable for this method, whereas the other liquid-liquid pairs listed have boiling point differences that are too small.
